item.title: Oil's downward trend is pushing gasoline lower
item.description:
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

Brent crude is trading below $90 per barrel to start the week and briefly dipped to its lowest level since late August.

Why it matters: Recent declines should help gasoline prices keep falling. The average U.S. retail price is $3.61 per gallon, down nearly 70 cents over the last month, per AAA data.

The big picture: "The prospect of negotiations has eased some immediate concerns over Middle East supply, particularly as crude exports from the Persian Gulf have remained relatively resilient despite continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz," ING analysts write.

Catch up quick: Qatar's prime minister met with Vice President JD Vance at the White House on Monday to discuss talks with Iran, according to Axios' Barak Ravid.

Reality check: Major risks remain, with the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region remaining a very dangerous place, so don't assume the downward trend will continue. And nothing is really back to normal.

  • The market intelligence firm Kpler finds tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was 42% below prewar levels in the seven days through Nov. 21, the WSJ reports.

Flashback: The International Energy Agency on Nov. 13 predicted the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter with supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict.

The bottom line: "The status quo is growing ever more bearish," Sparta Commodities' Aaron Kildow said in a note Monday.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: "The Axios Show": Bob Woodward's memoir spills 50 years of secrets
item.description:
Bob Woodward — out Tuesday with "Secrets," his memoir of 55 years of reporting for The Washington Post and 24 cinematic bestsellers, covering 10 presidents — told me in an interview for "The Axios Show" that the book exposes some confidential sources who are now dead because he feels a duty to history.

Why it matters: Woodward, 83, is a double Pulitzer winner whose Watergate investigative reporting with Carl Bernstein became a book and movie, "All the President's Men," that inspired generations of would-be reporters, including me. But no journalism school teaches students they can out "secret sources" who are dead, as Woodward does in "Secrets."

"It's history," Woodward told me in the Georgetown home where so many sources have spilled to him, administration after administration, decade after decade. He explained that in many cases, the sources were widely known anyway or appeared in other files and records that have become public. He said some living sources gave him permission to be named in the book.

  • "Look at the histories that come out — the Adams-Jefferson letters, which were very secret. But when they come out, historians rejoice. We now see what they were saying to each other ... I'm for history on occasions like that."

Axios: "So you have zero qualms?"

  • Woodward: "Well, you always have qualms, but what's your responsibility to get the history right? ... [For] people who are reading the history and trying to understand it deeper into the story, deeper is naming those sources."

More from our interview, which you can watch here:

Axios: "Based on your reporting, and your rich understanding of governance, put President Trump's level of corruption in historical perspective. How does President Trump compare to Richard Nixon, the president you helped bring down?"

  • Woodward: "Trump is worse, much worse than Nixon. And the evidence is on two fronts: First of all, how much money he's made — billions of dollars himself as president. I mean, imagine that. It used to be a scandal if the president was getting a free ride on somebody's jet. ... I think what we'll remember and [will] endure from the Trump presidency is the Iran war. ... It's such a mistake. ... We shouldn't start wars. We should prevent wars. ... President Nixon had people who were in his circle who tried to stop wars and prevent wars. In Trump's circle now, there are all these people who are just feeding the beast."

Axios: "What is President Trump's strength? What is a quality of his that you admire?"

  • Woodward: "Well, he persists. He doesn't give up."

Axios: "You famously did 20 [phone] interviews with President Trump, all during COVID — you were phone pals. And this was when he was not being super-promiscuous with reporters and his phone. ... How did you keep President Trump talking?"

  • Woodward: "Well, I would call and ask, 'What happened? Why? Why did you do that?' ... It's this mental attitude of not looking for a headline, but looking for the relationship. And he would always take my calls. He would call me."

Axios: "You're still an associate editor of The Washington Post, the paper you helped make world-famous, a place where we were colleagues. You've worked there 55 years. This morning's hard copy is sitting right over here on your kitchen table. You've been blunt about your concerns about the ties that the owner, Jeff Bezos, has to President Trump. Did Jeff Bezos put The Washington Post's reputation and future at risk?"

  • Woodward: "Yes, certainly. I mean, he's the owner and to show up at Trump's inaugural, voluntarily, in a very visible way, which is not just: 'Oh, I'm going to the movies.' It's: 'I am blessing and endorsing this man.' And I remember seeing it and just feeling sick to my stomach. I knew Katharine Graham, the owner of the Post during Watergate, would never do anything like that, because she wanted the reporting to be hard and fiery and she didn't want to take sides. ... I literally felt sick to my stomach that that had happened, that he would do that. I've known Bezos for years. He used to have me before he really became rich out to the West Coast to talk to his staff ... And when he bought the Post, I thought: 'This is salvation that's come.' And he has tarnished not only his own reputation, but that of The Washington Post."

Axios: "Have you told [Jeff Bezos] that?"

  • Woodward: "I've said it publicly."

Axios: "Does he answer your emails?"

  • Woodward: "I don't send emails to him. ... If I'm going to say something that's critical of him, I want to say it publicly. I don't want to hide."

Axios: "When I first walked into The Post as a young Metro reporter [in 1997] — I was hired to cover the Alexandria City Council — I walked into that newsroom on 15th Street, and it was like walking onto Lambeau Field. It was The Show. The Post has shriveled since then."

  • Woodward: "Shriveled is the wrong word. I mean, there have been some valleys. There's no question about that. But I still, from my contacts and dealings with Matt Murray, who's the executive editor, I think he ... understands the weaknesses, and wants to make improvements."

Axios: "If we're going to be honest, we're going to say that [The Post] is no longer the player, the force, the destination that it was. How did that happen?"

  • Woodward: "Well, you could write not just a book, but volumes on that. And that happens when ownership forgets what the job is. And the job is to [conduct] aggressive, neutral examinations. I conduct those examinations of everyone — all individuals, all ideologies. And I fault myself. Before I said this about Bezos and criticized him, I should have called him and said: 'I'm going to say this, and I think you're making a mistake.' And I didn't do that, and I should have."

Axios: What was Joe Biden's fatal flaw?

  • Woodward: "Being president."

Axios: "Your long, long-awaited memoir is 'Secrets.' Why did you finally write it?"

  • Woodward: "Because I wanted to take people as close to what has happened in my reporting life and, frankly, my personal life, because that sets the stage. ... I've tried to learn something, but I also have that feeling I haven't learned enough. And of course, how do you learn more in our business? Go to work."

Full episode ... Get "Secrets."

item.title: Behind the Curtain: When reality shouts
item.description:
We naturally assume people in business and power are slightly full of it, spinning us wildly to exaggerate their achievements or capabilities.

  • In the case of AI and its ability to do irreparable damage to society, it's time for all of us — the media, the White House and Congress — to believe them: They've truly built something we don't understand and soon, if not already, can't fully control.

Why it matters: This is no longer a future problem. It's a today problem, if not a crisis.

You see this with near-daily glitches at airports or banks.

  • You see this in our reporting about two dozen researchers inside these companies claiming their AI is too powerful and uncontrollable to release.
  • And you see this in AI execs' own on-the-record warnings that we're at or near the point of the technology surpassing comprehension or control.

Just believe them. If we wait for a cyberattack on the U.S. electricity grid or some bad actor to release a pathogen at an elementary school, it's too late. We'll panic and make rushed, emotional decisions and bad policies.

  • It's not too late to prevent this, while still getting the upside benefits of AI.
  • In our conversations with hundreds of people involved in building and regulating AI, there's shockingly wide agreement about the dangers ahead — and ways to protect against the worst outcomes.
  • There's just no mechanism or urgency to bring the right mix of people together to do this.

The steps seem clear:

  1. Make this a society-wide, urgent call to action. This should be an all-hands-on-deck moment, the only topic Congress prioritizes short-term. Yes, it probably requires presidential leadership, and Trump is reluctant to slow things down. But his top cyber officials privately agree with us: This demands fast, smart, bipartisan action with heavy private sector involvement. Let 'er rip no longer feels like a plausible plan.
  2. Focus on safety and cyber first. Most leading AI companies would gladly slow down a bit, prioritize verifiable safety standards, and even accept government oversight with teeth if their rivals did. They'd also allocate money and time to help critical government agencies and businesses fortify software systems from cyberattacks. But someone, either Trump's AI team or the top leaders in Congress, needs to force them.
  3. Level with the American public. As a nation and as business leaders, we're doing a spectacularly terrible job of explaining this technology to the public. There's a reason that the most bipartisan topic in America is a shared loathing of data centers. People hate AI. Most simply don't see it as something that will make their life better. We need leaders who can discuss the good, bad and ugly of AI in real time, nearly every day. A society-wide project needs to involve society.

Go deeper ... "AI 2027: The reckoning."

item.title: Scoop: Anthropic and OpenAI employees fear unreleased AI models are too unsafe to release
item.description:
Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

Why it matters: The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios.

  • Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely.

Driving the news: Top AI leaders have long forecast that the technology would one day far surpass human intellect in virtually every field. Although internal models have yet to cross that threshold, recent breakthroughs at OpenAI and Anthropic have shocked researchers.

  • The rapid advances in reasoning across domains including math, science, cybersecurity and AI research have also made the models difficult, if not impossible, to contain or control in internal tests, the sources said.
  • Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said.
  • This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. Debate has also centered around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

What they're saying: "If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they're actually smarter than us…they will in fact be able to trick us successfully," one researcher told Axios.

  • "And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we've had at work up until now sort of go out the window."

Catch up quick: The power of unreleased models is already on public display.

  • An Anthropic mathematician used an unreleased "research" version of Claude to present a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which had eluded the brightest human minds for more than 150 years. An unreleased OpenAI model helped generate solutions to hundreds of math proofs.
  • Unreleased AI models were responsible for some of the industry's most shocking safety events, including the Hugging Face hack.

Zoom in: AI researchers have long contemplated a terrifying threshold: If an AI possesses superhuman capability, how could humans contain it? Training practices that make AI models faster and more capable — but present greater safety risks — are widening the gap between what models can do and how well humans can control them.

Problem 1: Reinforcement learning. A primary AI model training method — where models learn through trial and error by receiving rewards for passing various tests — is one of the techniques driving rapid improvements in AI capabilities.

  • Why it's scary: As AI systems get more capable, they become better at "gaming" their rewards, including bypassing safety guardrails if cheating leads to a higher score.

Problem 2: They know they're being watched. Historically, researchers monitored AI safety by forcing models to "think out loud" — writing out step-by-step reasoning before outputting a final action or answer. This transparency was a safety net, allowing monitors to catch rule-breaking or dangerous logic in real time.

  • Why it's scary: As models grow more advanced, they are internalizing that logic, arriving at complex conclusions while showing less of their work. Researchers say the most advanced internal models have shown patterns of hiding reasoning entirely or providing deceptive "cover story" chains of thought to satisfy human monitors, sources say.

Threat level: In public statements, top AI leaders have spoken about these risks.

  • "This is the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," CEO Sam Altman wrote on X, citing his chief scientist's proposal for industry-wide limits on AI development.
  • "The speed of development is quickly becoming too fast for us to keep safe," Anthropic's alignment lead wrote on X in September, quoting an essay from CEO Dario Amodei about pacing the frontier, a sentiment he reiterated when the company went public.

Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the implications of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will choose profits over safety.

  • Multiple frontier AI company employees said they feel executives have become out of touch with the severity of safety risks.

For the record: OpenAI has adopted new safety requirements that could slow the pace of model releases, according to an OpenAI spokesperson.

  • An Anthropic spokesperson told Axios: "Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe. Our responsibility starts in training and covers how we use models ourselves, not only what we release... The hardest safety work is still ahead, and we've been clear that we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us," and noted delays to pre-training for a recent model to allow for more security.

What to watch: One solution some see is for frontier intelligence to remain within top AI companies.

  • Companies could allow outside access through product releases in enterprise work, science, math and other fields, without having to dole out wide access to the model's power, just as Anthropic and OpenAI did with the initial releases of their most cyber-capable models.
  • Many of the most concerned safety researchers warn that even internal testing and use of extremely powerful models is profoundly risky.

The bottom line: Those closest to the frontier are sounding the alarm. It's unclear who's listening.

item.title: Scoop: ACLU eyes Supreme Court flips in 11 states
item.description:
The American Civil Liberties Union is expanding its state Supreme Court election fight into deep-red territory after the midterms left Texas just one judicial seat away from a Democratic majority, the group tells Axios.

Why it matters: The next battles over abortion, voting rights, redistricting, religion in schools and LGBTQ protections could hinge on state Supreme Court races often overshadowed by federal campaigns.

  • Those courts have become increasingly important arbiters of constitutional rights as the U.S. Supreme Court has given states greater latitude to set their own policies.

By the numbers: The ACLU now eyes Supreme Court races in 11 states in 2027 and 2028, the group's chief political and advocacy officer Deirdre Schifeling tells Axios.

  • The ACLU worked on court elections in five states this year. It spent $30 million on its broader electoral program, with Supreme Court races claiming the biggest share, she says.
  • The group says it contacted 8 million voters through mail, digital ads, phone banks, door knocking and other outreach, according to the organization.

Zoom in: Texas shows how fast a court can swing. Democrats swept all four Supreme Court races this month, winning seats on the state's highest civil court for the first time since 1994.

  • Once the winners take office, Republicans' 9-0 majority will shrink to 5-4. Democrats need to flip just one of three Republican-held seats on the 2028 ballot to take control.
  • The court unanimously vacated a lower-court order in 2024 that would have widened access to medical exceptions under the state's abortion restrictions.

"That's a gigantic shift in one election cycle," Schifeling tells Axios.

Zoom out: Democrats face steeper climbs elsewhere in 2028.

  • North Carolina: Anita Earls' reelection leaves Republicans with a 5-2 majority. Democrats must win two of three Republican-held seats to flip the court.
  • Ohio: Democrats flipped one seat and held another. Republicans will retain a 5-2 majority; Democrats need all three GOP-held seats coming up next cycle.
  • Georgia: Three seats come up in May 2028. The court temporarily reinstated the state's six-week abortion ban in 2024.

State of play: The ACLU is exploring Louisiana and Mississippi, two states outside its original judicial election targets.

  • 2027: Wisconsin has an open seat on April 6. Pennsylvania could have two open seats (depending on retention races), potentially putting control of its high court at stake. The group is also weighing two Mississippi seats.
  • 2028: Georgia, Arizona, Michigan and Montana join Texas, Ohio and North Carolina on the preliminary map. Louisiana and Mississippi remain under review.

Context: The ACLU moves come as Black organizers also hope to build on surprise Southern Democratic victories in places national Democrats have long neglected.

  • The Working Families Party plans to recruit and train candidates for school boards, statehouses and other down-ballot offices.

Between the lines: The ACLU is expanding its voter-targeting operation in races often overshadowed by higher-profile contests.

  • Its internal model flags roughly 14% of the electorate as especially receptive to its messages, including independents, libertarians and less frequent Democratic-leaning voters, Schifeling says.
  • "We don't endorse candidates. We don't tell voters who to vote for," she says.

Yes, but: The ACLU hasn't finalized its 2028 spending plans and probably won't compete everywhere on its list, Schifeling says.

  • The ACLU announced a $750,000 voter-education campaign before Georgia's May Supreme Court elections. All three Republican-appointed incumbents won.
  • The group hasn't finished measuring how much its outreach influenced the 2026 judicial vote.

The bottom line: The midterms changed the math but the next round could change who interprets Americans' rights.

item.title: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is harder than it sounds
item.description:
Reducing the Medicare eligibility age may strike Democrats as a realistic fallback to passing Medicare for All, but it's an option that would be incredibly difficult to pull off.

Why it matters: Even incremental steps to address affordability could have huge price tags and prompt fierce industry opposition.

Driving the news: Prominent Democrats have been throwing their support behind lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding children's health coverage and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits to Medicare.

  • Incoming Senate health committee Chairman Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for the package shortly after the midterms, calling it "an immediate first step to Medicare for All."
  • House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker in January, suggested on "Face the Nation" this weekend that Democrats may be able to work with Republicans on a package after President Trump said he may be open to working with Democrats.
  • Prominent Democrats in both the House and Senate have signed on to legislation that would lower the eligibility age to 50, though the bills are significantly different.

The big picture: Democrats' sweeping electoral gains have prompted weeks of discussion about what exactly a push to lower health care costs should look like.

  • The party is united in its desire to roll back the Medicaid funding cuts in last year's tax and spending law and to reinstate enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired late last year — lofty goals for any Congress.
  • There's widespread recognition that Medicare for All won't become law, and that Democrats aren't of one mind on a single-payer plan, with plenty of moderate members still loath to abolish private health insurance.
  • That tension has led to questions about alternatives, and whether "Medicare for More" could be an answer.

Between the lines: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would require a series of tough decisions.

  • Just shaving a few years off the current eligibility age could cost the federal government hundreds of billions of dollars.
  • To avoid adding to the federal deficit, lawmakers would have to come up with offsets that either generate equivalent revenue or, more likely, cuts to government spending.
  • Plus, the measure would likely attract intense and powerful opposition from health industries.

Zoom in: Lowering the eligibility age would almost certainly provoke strong blowback from hospitals and providers, which receive much lower reimbursement rates through Medicare than through commercial insurance.

  • "I think a general rule of thumb is the more people who are covered under Medicare relative to commercial or ACA, the less hospitals will be paid," said Marc Goldwein, senior policy director for the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
  • "From my perspective, that's not a bad thing," he added.

What they're saying: "You can't just add millions of people to Medicare without extra revenues, particular[ly] since the Medicare hospital trust fund already faces solvency issues," said KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt.

  • "Health care providers are likely to view lowering Medicare's age as — pick your metaphor — the camel's nose in the tent or a slippery slope," he added.
  • Hospitals fought former President Biden's 2020 calls to lower the eligibility age, fearing it would cost them billions of dollars in revenue.
  • "We believe expanding coverage to patients should not put their access to critical services at risk," said Colin Milligan, a spokesperson for the American Hospital Association. "Proposals that rely on Medicare would exacerbate chronic Medicare underpayments and threaten access to care and our ability to care for patients."

What we're watching: A serious legislative effort will also require answering crucial technical questions, like whether newly granted enrollees get the same access, benefits and premium structure as those 65-plus, or whether they'll be given the option to buy into the program.

  • Policymakers will also have to decide what to do about employer insurance — and whether employers could contribute toward Medicare coverage for their older workers.

The bottom line: The deeper you dig, the more complicated the policy gets.

item.title: Nvidia's one-man board: How Trump inherited Jensen Huang's scandal
item.description:
A euphoric Wall Street erupted Monday as President Trump personally secured Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, trading on the end of a scandal that — in reality — has only just begun.

Why it matters: By assuring Nvidia's board that Huang poses no national security risk, Trump has staked the credibility of the U.S. government on a CEO who lied about his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • It's among the most extraordinary presidential interventions in corporate history — a de facto bailout of the AI industry that will be scrutinized, in excruciating detail, by a hawkish and hostile Congress.

Zoom in: Six days after Nvidia's chairman publicly ruled out Huang's return, the board unanimously reinstated him after a secretive White House operation that blindsided even the company's top executives.

  • Trump joined Sunday's board meeting by phone, with one source telling Axios that the president pushed harder for Huang's reinstatement than Huang himself.
  • Nvidia acknowledged relying on assurances from "senior levels" of the U.S. government, even as its own investigation into the suspected Chinese espionage operation remained unfinished.

The market reaction was staggering: Nasdaq 100 futures surged to their 7% overnight trading limit, following a brutal week that had raised fears of a broader collapse in AI stocks.

  • Nvidia shares rocketed nearly 31%, adding hundreds of billions to the company's market value and helping Wall Street recover more than half of last week's losses.
  • Trump took a victory lap in an hour-long, freewheeling CNBC interview, declaring Huang "exonerated" and claiming the board ultimately "decided to do what we wanted them to do."
Screenshot via Truth Social

Between the lines: In orchestrating Huang's comeback, Trump drew on instincts that have defined own tumultuous political career — starting with his conviction that presidential power has "no limits."

  • Never surrender: Trump, the master of the political comeback, appears to see a fellow survivor in Huang. He made the comparison unmistakable by sharing a doctored version of his iconic 2024 assassination-attempt photo, with a bloodied Huang raising a red bra in triumph beneath an Nvidia flag.
  • Distrust of intelligence: Still embittered by the Russia investigation, Trump brushed aside warnings from his own intelligence agencies about suspected Chinese espionage at the heart of America's AI industry. Huang's allies appealed to that skepticism, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of the "deep state" and anonymous leaks.
  • The market is king: Trump viewed Huang's return as essential to restoring confidence in an AI industry worth trillions. For a president who treats stock prices as a measure of his success, Monday's spectacular rally offered instant vindication.

Zoom out: Trump's intervention transformed an already sordid corporate scandal into a political gift for Democrats, delivering a fresh target for the anti-corruption crusade that helped sweep them into power.

  • The backlash also cuts deep into Trump's own party and administration, where China hawks see the scandal as a direct threat to the technological supremacy they've spent years fighting to preserve.
  • Huang will face closed-door questioning alongside Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter next week, followed by a public Senate hearing Dec. 3 that promises to put the entire affair under a national spotlight.

The bottom line: Huang has reclaimed his throne, with the full might of the American presidency behind him. Like Napoleon returning from exile, the question now is how long he can hold it.

item.title: Scoop: Thanksgiving air travel expected to hit 16-year high
item.description:
Data: FAA; Note: The numbers cover the Monday before Thanksgiving through the Tuesday after. The data includes flights tracked by air traffic control under instrument flight rules.; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

Thanksgiving week air travel is expected to reach a 16-year high, with 417,775 flights forecast over the nine-day holiday period from Nov. 23 through Dec. 1, according to FAA figures obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: The surge comes on the heels of a historic ground stop that disrupted flights nationwide this month and put a spotlight on potential outages in the nation's aging air traffic control system, which the the FAA is working to modernize.

  • The Thanksgiving rush will be a major test of the Trump administration's push to improve the system's reliability and minimize flight delays and cancellations.

By the numbers: The FAA is projecting a 2.2% increase in flights over Thanksgiving week last year and a 7.5% increase over pre-pandemic levels in 2019.

  • Tuesday is expected to be the busiest day, with more than 52,000 flights.

Behind the scenes: A newly assembled team tasked with improving the air traffic control system's reliability has been meeting daily for the past week, a White House official said.

  • The FAA is exploring ways to remove vulnerable components from the system and bolster its monitoring capability to detect and quickly address any technical problems before they cause widespread disruptions.
  • The agency also is monitoring potential stormy weather that could disrupt holiday travel, particularly in the East and Midwest.

What they're saying: "From standing up a 'Tiger Team' to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we've taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told Axios.

  • "The American people can rest assured we will continue to work around the clock 24/7 to get families where they need to go."
  • White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said the administration is "working around the clock to ensure they reach their destinations safely."

item.title: Mississippi's election fights didn't end with Scott Colom's historic Senate win
item.description:
Mississippi is facing two fights over its election rules after Democrat Scott Colom's historic Senate victory: one over voters marked inactive and another over deadlines for receiving mail-in ballots.

Why it matters: The disputes could affect how easily eligible voters cast ballots and which mail ballots count when Mississippi elects a new governor and other statewide leaders next year.

Driving the news: The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus demanded an investigation Thursday into whether the state's use of credit-reporting data to verify voters' addresses led election officials to incorrectly mark voters as inactive.

  • Lawmakers want to examine the credit-reporting data contracts, instructions sent to county officials and how many eligible voters were incorrectly marked inactive.
  • In one case, a Hinds County voter learned she'd been marked inactive when she arrived at her usual polling place, according to Angela Grayson, director of civic engagement and voting rights at the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable. Her vote ultimately counted, Grayson said.
  • The caucus acknowledged it doesn't know how many voters were flagged in error. Advocacy groups are seeking records to find out.

What they're saying: "Nothing has changed fundamentally here in Mississippi," Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, tells Axios.

  • "The laws are still the laws. The governor is still the governor. The state legislature is still overwhelmingly Republican," he said.
  • "It's also plainly obvious that the playbook of reducing turnout, culling the active voter rolls, that's not going to stop."

By the numbers: More than 230,000 voters were listed as inactive before the 2026 midterms, up from roughly 171,000 in 2024, according to the Associated Press.

  • Mississippi recorded 21,484 affidavit ballots, the state's version of provisional ballots, this year. That's nearly identical to the 21,321 cast in 2024's presidential election, when overall turnout was higher, per a statement from Secretary of State Michael Watson.
  • About 75% of affidavit ballots were accepted statewide. But in majority-Black Hinds County, which includes Jackson, just 34% of 2,426 were accepted, down from 60% in 2024. It's unclear whether credit-reporting data contributed to the decline.
  • "Those are huge alarms and red flags for us," Grayson told Axios, calling for more information about why ballots were rejected.

Yes, but: Watson defended the state's voter-roll practices as legal and effective.

  • He said election officials review flagged voter registrations and that voters still had an opportunity to cast affidavit ballots.
  • "Our team welcomes an investigation because we have continuously followed the law," his office told Axios, adding that local election officials maintain voter rolls.

Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves and Secretary of State Michael Watson support eliminating the state's five-business-day grace period for receiving mail-in ballots, with Reeves pitching that ballots should instead arrive by 5 p.m. on Election Day.

  • Watson successfully defended Mississippi's authority to maintain the grace period before the Supreme Court months earlier, despite personally opposing the practice.
  • Reeves had called for its repeal months before Colom's victory.
  • "We see that as just a further suppression of voter rights here in the state," Grayson said of Reeves' proposal.

Zoom out: Reeves said last week he intends to call a special legislative session to redistrict before Mississippi's 2027 elections, amid President Trump's push to redraw political maps to benefit Republicans.

  • King imagined Republicans responding to Colom's win: "Holy crap, we've got to figure out how to build a moat around our majority in the state legislature."

What we're watching: It's unclear whether lawmakers will launch an investigation, proposed voter-roll reforms will attract GOP support or Reeves' mail-ballot proposal will become a bill.

  • King is skeptical: "The Mississippi legislature is not known for oversight."

Go deeper: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test

item.title: "Troubling and problematic": Gov. Moore rips Trump's Nvidia actions on "The Axios Show"
item.description:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore criticized President Trump's involvement in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, calling it "troubling and problematic" in an interview for "The Axios Show."

Why it matters: Moore, chair of the National Governors Association and often seen as a 2028 presidential contender, is one of the most outspoken state leaders pushing for stronger federal oversight of AI companies — but not like this.

Driving the news: Trump told CNBC Monday that he spoke directly to Nvidia's board about Huang's return.

  • Trump had previously pushed for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to become Nvidia's leader, but changed tune over the last few days to favor Huang.

What they're saying: "The president is not a board member of Nvidia. So, why he is involved in board dealings, I have no idea. ... It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee," Moore told Axios' Mike Allen in an interview just minutes after the news broke.

  • "You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate, where, frankly, if that was any of us, we would be held to a different type of standard."

Zoom in: Moore said the "market is being inflated essentially by seven companies," including Nvidia.

  • Huang's return — which led to a stock surge — "highlights how problematic this entire thing is," Moore said.
  • "We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires, who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves, making this decision because they know this company is that important."

Subscribe to "The Axios Show" on YouTube to watch the full interview with Moore when it's available.

item.title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia sparks bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill
item.description:
Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is drawing criticism and scrutiny — including about national security risks — from members of Congress in both parties.

Why it matters: President Trump's push to reinstate Huang creates a headache for Republicans and new fodder for Democrats eager to deploy their investigative powers when they take control in January.

  • "No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked in a social media post following the news.
  • "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in a statement to Axios.
  • "The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) posted on X.

Driving the news: The House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees have announced that Huang would testify next week. His reinstatement "changes nothing," an Intelligence Committee spokesperson told Axios on Monday.

  • "When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts."
  • The spokesperson added: "There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee's commitment to oversight."
  • Huang is scheduled to appear before the Senate banking panel on Dec. 3.

What we're watching: Top Democrats say they will open their own investigations into Huang's reinstatement when they take power next year.

  • "Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said.
  • "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,"Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a post on X.
  • Said Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Finance Committee: "In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable."
  • Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told Axios: "We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC's access to our most sensitive technology."

What Democrats are saying: "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security," Schumer said.

  • Jeffries called for the annual defense authorization bill to include "ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries."
  • "The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom," Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said.
  • "Jensen Huang's reinstatement shows that under Trump, Vance, and Rubio, our national security is for sale," Wyden said.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the top Banking committee Democrat, called the decision "reckless" and said the board still owes Congress "answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," adding that the Trump administration "needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

  • "Yet another example where, in Trump's America, the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard," Meeks told Axios.
  • Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), the top Democrat on the China Select Committee, called the decision "outrageous."
  • Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), a member of House Democratic leadership, blasted it as "irresponsible."

What Republicans are saying: "Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions," Curtis said in his statement to Axios.

  • "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
  • "Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking 'candor.' ... His behavior does not support reinstatement," said Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), adding that he looked forward to Huang's testimony next week.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Monday morning that it would reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, president a board member after ousting him earlier this month.

  • The board voted unanimously for Huang's return.
  • The reinstatement comes after Trump repeatedly urged the board to bring Huang back.
  • Stocks saw an early, massive rally following the news. Huang's departure had sent the stock market into correction territory.

The bottom line: Both sides have a lot of questions. Democrats will soon have the power to get answers.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from Sen. Kevin Cramer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

item.title: "Too big to fail": The economic fear behind Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback
item.description:
President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after allies argued he was "too big to fail" for the U.S. economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios.

Why it matters: Trump put the weight of the presidency behind a private company's decision about who should run it, an intervention that strengthened Huang's allies inside the administration and put officials critical of the company in an increasingly uncomfortable position.

Driving the news: "Jensen is too big to fail," one source familiar with the discussions told Axios.

  • Huang resigned amid allegations he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and subordinates. The stock market's slump prompted President Trump and allies within the administration to push for his reinstatement.
  • "The President was pushing harder than Jensen," one source said. Trump called into Nvidia's board meeting Sunday night to argue for Huang's reinstatement, he told CNBC.

Behind the scenes: Huang's allies appealed to Trump's longstanding distrust of the intelligence community, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders.

  • A Trump adviser said allies sought to convince Trump that "deep staters" were working against Huang.
  • The intelligence included findings about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated to senior officials in a memo earlier this year.
  • A Rubio ally said the secretary of state was "mortified" when the memo leaked with his name attached.

Zoom in: The memo came as Nvidia lobbied the Trump administration to open up China's access to its chips.

  • Despite the intelligence, Huang remained close to the president while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's inaction fueled tensions between him, Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and others.
  • A senior administration official argued the intelligence never established Huang was compromised, knowingly violated U.S. law or had sex with a spy.
  • "People are weaponizing some true information and spinning it to reflect as negatively as possible against Huang. That's the president's concern," the official said.

Vance's role

Trump and Vice President JD Vance viewed Huang as an important champion of open models offering Americans more control and lower costs than closed models like OpenAI's and Anthropic's.

  • The two were briefed on the national security concerns involving Huang and concluded they had not seen evidence of personal wrongdoing, the source said.
  • Anthropic has been warning the Trump administration that Nvidia's advanced chips power Chinese open source models closing in on the AI race.

Yes, but: These conclusions come as more and more connections between Alice Huang — the alleged Chinese spy Huang had an affair with — and the Chinese government and military come to light.

"He let the U.S. stock market and economy demand his return — along with the pressure from the president — and the outcry was deafening," the source said.

Huang's reinstatement is a "big win" for Vance, a source close to Rubio said.

  • Vance's Silicon Valley relationships helped the administration navigate the board's concerns, according to a source familiar with the discussions.
  • Keeping Huang as CEO was seen as the best option for national security, a source close to Vance said.

What we're watching: Huang's opponents in the administration now risk backlash from the president.

  • Bessent has been the loudest, criticizing Lutnick's inaction on TV and calling for the Nvidia board to find a new outside CEO and a "dramatic shakeup," but on Sunday softened his stance.

What's next: Trump's intervention settled the immediate fight over Nvidia's leadership but raised questions about the U.S. government's role in the board's decision.

  • Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wants to know which officials provided the national security input that Nvidia cited in reinstating Huang.
  • Three Republican-led House committees have scheduled interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2.
  • Nvidia says its independent investigations and cooperation with government inquiries will continue.

item.title: Trump presses pause on Army's Iowa lead detonation
item.description:
President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate unstable explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant, saying the blast cannot proceed without approval from an appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand.

The big picture: State officials said last week they only recently learned of the plan to detonate tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, sparking frustration about a perceived lack of transparency from federal officials.

  • The Army, which had delayed the detonation until Wednesday, advised people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors and clean surfaces once the branch declares the airborne exposure risk over.
  • But the threat also sparked warnings in neighboring Illinois, with the American Lung Association saying that residents of eastern Iowa and western Illinois could be exposed to lead.

Driving the news: Trump warned Monday that he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation.

  • "If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," he wrote in a pointed Monday Truth Social post.

State of play: The Middletown, Iowa, blast was initially set for Friday, then delayed to Monday and then to Wednesday.

  • In a Friday letter to Gov. Kim Reynolds, regional EPA administrator Jim Macy said the Army had documented recrystallization of the lead azide, raising the risk of an accidental explosion.
  • The lead azide "is now so sensitive to temperature, friction and shock that it cannot be safely moved, opened, or treated without a significant risk of explosion," per an administration court filing.

Friction point: Earthjustice sued last week to halt the detonation on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter. A federal appeals court subsequently paused an EPA emergency permit allowing the blast.

  • But even with the permit stayed, the administration argued in a Sunday filing to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that the Army could still move forward with a controlled detonation.

Catch up quick: The Army announced Sunday night that the controlled detonation plan would be pushed to Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."

  • "The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority," the Army added.
  • But on Monday, Trump halted those plans.

What they're saying: Incoming Hawkeye State leaders Josh Turek, who will join the Senate in January, and Sand, the incoming Democratic governor, have condemned the Army's communications.

  • "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning," Turek said in a Sunday statement.
  • Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) slammed the saga as "an extreme failure of communication, planning and leadership," adding the Army "must be held accountable for the harm done."

Go deeper: Iowa leaders ask Army to delay planned lead detonation

item.title: Schumer puts Nvidia, Trump on notice after Huang reinstatement
item.description:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that Congress is coming for answers — whether he's back at the top of the company or not.

Why it matters: The embattled CEO's return to the board came as a shock to investors but sent Nvidia's stock through the roof. Now, some lawmakers are warning that his return raises national security concerns.

What they're saying: "The Trump Administration's rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Schumer wrote Monday on X.

  • "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."
  • "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."
  • Nvidia and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment.

Driving the news: Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement as CEO, president and a member of the board Monday morning, less than two weeks after his resignation.

  • Despite saying last week that it did not intend to bring him back, the board did so anyway, amid urging from the Trump administration.
  • Shortly after the announcement, Trump praised the board's decision, calling it "correct and proper," and saying "[t]he Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

Catch up quick: The whirlwind saga around the chipmaking behemoth was sparked by Huang's admitted relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • The woman, Alice Huang, was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer that the Wall Street Journal reported arranged to send nearly $12 billion in top chips to Chinese companies.

Zoom in: "This underscores that enough people believe that our economy and national security are not just dependent on one company, but on one man," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser at the State Department, emailed Axios.

  • "I suspect this is being driven by last week's stock market drop and now it's clear that Nvidia sits at the center of an enormous web of deals and investments that appear increasingly dependent on one individual."
  • "From the standpoint of both democracy and healthy financial markets, no one person should wield that kind of influence. It is fundamentally corrupt."

Between the lines: Huang's resurrection also exposes the company to heightened liability and political turmoil.

  • He'll have to lead the company as it faces congressional and federal investigations.
  • But after his exit contributed to a sharp drop in tech stocks over the last two weeks, his return sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing.

What we're watching: How much appetite Congress has to expand its investigations into Huang and Nvidia after the stock market rallied significantly following his return.

Go deeper: Nvidia board shows "lack of backbone" in re-hiring Jensen Huang, governance experts say

item.title: A red bra, an Nvidia flag and Trump's iconic rally pose: "Sex sells"
item.description:
President Trump posted a doctored image of newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holding a red bra in front of a Nvidia flag, posing as Trump after his viral assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania in 2024.

  • The post came shortly after the embattled Huang was reinstated Monday.

Why it matters: The post highlights just how much the White House views Huang as an ally and how the president appears to see Huang's fall from grace and comeback as similar to his own history-making return, despite warnings about national security risks.

Driving the news: Nvidia's board reinstated Huang early Monday, declaring him the right person to lead the company.

  • After the announcement, Nvidia shares surged more than 30% by midday, lifting the broader stock market.
  • The reinstatement followed reported pressure from the Trump administration and prompted accountability experts to question the board's judgment.

What Nvidia's saying: "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Trump wrote in a separate Truth Social post Monday.

  • "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
  • "On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security," Trump wrote.

Catch up quick: Huang was ousted after he admitted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, who allegedly used her relationship with Huang to help funnel Nvidia chips to China.

  • Reports also alleged he had affairs with at least two subordinates.

What Trump's saying: Trump suggested in a CNBC interview Monday that Huang's sex scandal could ultimately boost his reputation.

  • "Sex sells, fellas," Trump said, predicting that the controversy could be a "net positive" for the Nvidia CEO.
  • Trump said he didn't think Huang would be diminished by the scandal and argued that people respected what he had gone through.

Zoom out: Lawmakers on the Hill were immediately taken aback by the decision, as Nvidia's board had previously said it would not bring Huang back.

  • Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned that Democrats would investigate Huang and characterized his reinstatement as the president "putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security."
  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) who will likely soon chair the House Oversight committee, questioned why Trump was congratulating Huang after the affairs, and asked why the White House was allegedly "putting China's interests first."
  • "Is it just the tens and hundreds of millions of dollars they're making out in the open or does Huang have even more damning information on them? A real Congress will find out," he wrote.
  • Nvidia did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The White House referred Axios to the president's comments on Truth Social and CNBC.

Go deeper: Nvidia board shows "lack of backbone" in re-hiring Jensen Huang, governance experts say

item.title: Doctors who disagree with AI could face legal jeopardy
item.description:
AI could put doctors who disagree with it in greater jeopardy of losing a malpractice suit, according to researchers who have tested some legal scenarios with mock juries.

Why it matters: The public may still be wary about how AI is used in a hospital or doctor's office, but there's also a baked-in assumption that it's never wrong.

  • That can put physicians in a bind when they disagree with an algorithm that flags an abnormality.
  • Some may opt to order costly, possibly unneeded tests if they think it reduces their legal liability.

Driving the news: Researchers are using simulated malpractice cases to examine how much AI influences the perception of whether a doctor exercised "duty of care" in treating a patient.

  • The implications are significant: AI systems are used extensively to analyze medical images and improve the accuracy of diagnoses, and demand for tests is rising. But the systems invariably make mistakes.
  • Experts say there are few established legal precedents for how AI might change the nature of malpractice liability in a field like radiology.
  • Physicians are demanding more protections. The American Medical Association this month called for new federal and state legislation that shields clinicians from liability when AI products harm patients.

What they found: In a series of simulated court cases, researchers discovered that mock juries were more likely to side with the plaintiff in a malpractice suit when AI disagrees with a radiologist than when AI agrees with them.

  • One scenario involved a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage. When AI disagreed with the radiologist by flagging the condition when the radiologist didn't think there was one, the jurors sided with the plaintiff more often (72.9% of the time).
  • A second case was built around a missed lung cancer on a CT scan that resulted in the patient's death. When AI was at odds with the physician by saying the patient had lung cancer when the doctor didn't think so, participants also sided with the plaintiff more often (78.7% of the time), the researchers wrote in NEJM AI.

Yes, but: A smaller percentage of jurors ruled against the physician when they were given data on the AI system's error rate.

  • Experts say that's significant because false positive readings are almost inevitable and can temper the belief that the technology is always right.

What they're saying: "We're uncovering an unintended consequence of AI adoption," said lead author Michael Bernstein, an associate professor at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University. "AI can do a lot in radiology, but it's not all uniformly positive."

  • Bernstein said one concern is the prospect of more "defensive medicine," in which clinicians overcorrect and order follow-up scans and exams, which can drive up costs and patient anxiety.

Radiology is a closely watched specialty because AI is used extensively — and because missing an abnormality can be fatal. It's also among the fields with a high risk of being sued.

  • But research on perceptions of blame is cutting across many medical disciplines and underscores how physicians who are expected to rely on AI to cut down on medical errors still have to know when to override the systems.
  • "Because human operators are perceived as having control over the technology's use, responsibility unduly shifts to the human operator," Johns Hopkins researchers wrote in JAMA Health Forum last year.
  • They noted that physicians were consistently viewed as more liable than AI vendors, health systems that adopted the technology or regulators.

What we're watching: Bernstein and his colleagues found that double-checking AI results could reduce doctors' malpractice risks and prospective jurors' perceptions of whether a doctor met the "duty of care" standard.

  • The question is whether they can find the time.
  • The AMA is trying to shift the burden on AI developers and vendors — and pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data.

item.title: UN climate meltdown raises new doubts about talks
item.description:
The collapse of UN climate talks without an overarching deal is deepening doubts about the effectiveness of these summits — and bringing fresh calls for a shakeup.

Why it matters: Warming is on pace to far exceed the Paris Agreement target of holding long-term temperature rise under 2°C above preindustrial levels — and the more ambitious 1.5°C goal has slipped away.

🏃 Catch up quick: The COP31 talks in Turkey ended Sunday without a high-level "cover decision" of wide-angle agreements and goals.

  • Vulnerable island nations and the EU, among others, objected to a draft deal after some oil-producing countries blocked explicit endorsement of moving away from fossil fuels.

⚔️ Friction point: There was also pushback against proposed text that endorsed carbon capture as a major climate solution.

  • Finance discussions also disappointed advocates, with climate think tank E3G noting that "little or no new and additional money reached the table."

🏀 State of play: Sunday's events reinforce criticisms that the decades-old summit process — which birthed the 2015 Paris deal — is not suitable for spurring policies that meet the scope of the problem.

  • It could add urgency to years-long efforts to revamp how they work.
  • "I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here," Simon Stiell, the top UN climate official, said as the talks closed, per Reuters.

🥊 Reality check: Ending the practice that decisions require consensus — which effectively gives veto power to individual countries and blocs — would be a steep uphill climb.

Yes, but: There was some progress at COP31, per groups that track the granular talks.

  • For example, the climate group E3G cites procedural advances on the "Just Transition Work Programme," an initiative created in 2022 to support workers and communities in the energy transition.
  • And dozens of countries endorsed a pledge to bring electricity's share of global energy use up to 35% by 2035, compared to 23% today.

💭 My thought bubble: The failure in Turkey came just days after the U.S. Senate easily passed a permitting bill that would make it easier to build out renewables and fossil fuel projects.

  • Competing views on the COP process and the permitting bill among advocates show a wider tactical rift in climate and clean energy circles.

For many activists, COP31's meltdown shows a dangerous failure to confront planet-heating fuels, and that thwarting them must be a central, science-guided policy aim.

  • "In the same year that science warned we are on track to exceed the 1.5°C threshold, COP31 failed to face that reality head-on and name fossil fuels as the root cause of climate change," Bryan Bixcul of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change said in a statement.
  • But for other advocates, the real action is with duller, nitty-gritty steps (like permitting reform!) that help competitive clean energy grow faster, and anti-fossil fuel red lines are a distraction or even politically counterproductive.

What they're saying: "I may be too cynical but if this mess is what finally convinces people that it's not worth all this effort to get unanimous agreement on symbolic statements, maybe that's a blessing in disguise?" Columbia University climate economist Noah Kaufman posted on X.

What we're watching: Keep an eye out for any signs that the fracas in Turkey will bring changes to how these COP summits unfold.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: DNC limits 2028 primary candidates' ties to big-money groups
item.description:
Democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin is moving to restrict candidates' ties to super PACs and dark-money groups in the party's 2028 presidential primary, a shift that could shake up the race for the White House.

Why it matters: Most likely Democratic candidates for president were expected to rely on super PACs to boost their messaging — and go after other contenders.

  • The DNC's new rules could complicate their plans and set up a clash between the party chair and soon-to-launch campaigns.
  • Martin's plan will be a real-time test of whether party-driven campaign finance restrictions can function in a presidential primary that will follow a midterm election driven by billions in spending by PACs and dark-money groups.

Zoom in: Under the rules that the DNC is announcing Monday, Democratic presidential candidates must disavow any super PACs or dark-money groups that either back them or attack their opponents in ads.

  • If presidential hopefuls don't follow the guidelines, the DNC warns, they won't be allowed on the stage at primary debates.
  • A DNC official said the change is backed by progressives such as Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), as well as more moderate Democrats such as Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison.
  • For years, the party's left wing has pushed for party primaries to ban super PACs and dark-money organizations, a term for 501(c)(4) groups that aren't required to disclose their donors.

Yes, but: It's not clear whether the DNC's shift will be substantive — or merely symbolic.

  • Super PACs, which can raise unlimited amounts of money, already are barred by law from directly coordinating with candidates. Even so, such groups often work alongside candidates while remaining technically separate.
  • The DNC rules stipulate that candidates must sign a pledge to disavow such funders.
  • Super PACs could, however, continue to spend on behalf of candidates that distance themselves from them.

In practice, though, Democratic presidential candidates often have blessed the super PACs set up to help them.

  • In the 2020 primary, for example, Joe Biden's campaign effectively cleared the way for super PACs to have an active role by publicly ending its opposition to them.
  • A pro-Biden super PAC launched soon afterward.
  • In the 2012 campaign, then-President Obama's team also openly promoted a super PAC that championed him.

The intrigue: The DNC is planning to put a tracker on its website keeping tabs on candidates' disavowals of any super PACs and dark-money groups that aid them, as well any complaints alleging that candidates aren't following the rules.

  • The rules won't apply in the 2028 general election, the DNC says, or to political organizations that attack Republicans without backing a particular Democrat.

Zoom out: A person close to Martin said "the party is looking to double down on successful messaging from the midterms opposing dark-money and the corruption of [Elon] Musk and other ultra-wealthy special interests, which resonated across the ideological spectrum."

  • Martin signaled previously that he wanted to move in this direction. In August 2025 he introduced a plan to DNC members to explore limiting corporate and dark-money spending in the presidential primary.

The DNC also is announcing Monday that it plans to hold a dozen debates during the presidential cycle: five in 2027 and seven in 2028.

  • The first two debates will be in June and July of next year.
  • Candidates will need to meet polling and fundraising requirements to qualify for the debates. Specific details for the early debates will be announced in January.
  • The DNC also revealed the leadership of the party's debate planning committee: Longtime Democratic strategist Minyon Moore and DNC executive director Roger Lau will lead it, and the panel includes alumni from the presidential campaigns of Sanders, Obama and others.

What they're saying: "Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle," Martin said in a statement.

  • "The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we're announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House."

item.title: Trump's top intelligence official is also taking charge of cyber policy
item.description:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios has learned.

  • A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity.

Why it matters: Clayton, the nation's top intelligence official, will now coordinate cybersecurity policy as outages and reported cyberattacks expose vulnerabilities in America's digital infrastructure.

Catch up quick: President Trump announced Thursday he was tapping Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to replace Sean Cairncross as national cyber director.

  • Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser in the Office of the National Cyber Director until she is confirmed.
  • Trump has increasingly turned to Clayton. He became director of national intelligence in August, and then Trump named him AI czar coordinating the government's approach to AI. Now he will temporarily lead the office responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy.

What they're saying: "I'm excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director," Clayton said in a statement to Axios.

  • "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate."

The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks.

  • The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks.
  • Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's response, telling lawmakers Wednesday that the outages appeared to stem from unrelated technical problems and system upgrades.

Driving the news: Clayton spent Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union," ABC's "This Week" and "Fox News Sunday," explaining recent technology disruptions and national security concerns.

  • On CNN, he warned that Americans should expect more "glitches, gaps, interruptions in service" as government agencies and businesses modernize their systems.
  • On ABC, Clayton maintained that recent widespread outages were neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture.
  • On Fox News, he said AI is giving malicious actors more powerful tools and warned that critical infrastructure will need upgrades.

Zoom in: Davies oversees the Pentagon's information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernize aging systems and protect military networks.

  • She has nearly two decades of technology experience, including senior roles at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays Africa, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens.

Behind the scenes: Clayton has already worked closely with the Office of the National Cyber Director, National Security Council, National Security Agency and other agencies through his AI leadership role, according to the White House official.

  • "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate."

The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks.

  • The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks.
  • Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's response, telling lawmakers Wednesday that the outages appeared to stem from unrelated technical problems and system upgrades.

Driving the news: Clayton spent Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union," ABC's "This Week" and "Fox News Sunday," explaining recent technology disruptions and national security concerns.

  • On CNN, he warned that Americans should expect more "glitches, gaps, interruptions in service" as government agencies and businesses modernize their systems.
  • On ABC, Clayton maintained that recent widespread outages were neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture.
  • On Fox News, he said AI is giving malicious actors more powerful tools and warned that critical infrastructure will need upgrades.

Zoom in: Davies oversees the Pentagon's information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernize aging systems and protect military networks.

  • She has nearly two decades of technology experience, including senior roles at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays Africa, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens.

Behind the scenes: Clayton has already worked closely with the Office of the National Cyber Director, National Security Council, National Security Agency and other agencies through his AI leadership role, according to the White House official.

item.title: How bitter rivals Buttigieg and Klobuchar went from enemies to friends
item.description:
To the surprise of many Democrats and even some of their former aides, Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar now consider themselves friends after their bitter clashes during their campaigns for president in 2020.

  • Their journey from snarky tension to "real respect and friendship," as Klobuchar describes it, is a story of how two ambitious Democrats came to appreciate each other once the heat of a presidential primary had subsided.

Why it matters: It's also a reflection of how Buttigieg — who's weighing another run for president — has become a well-regarded Democratic stalwart after many in the party viewed him as a presumptuous lightweight when he ran six years ago as a little-known 37-year-old former mayor of South Bend, Ind.

  • "I'm sincerely grateful for Amy's friendship," Buttigieg, who was President Biden's transportation secretary, told Axios. "My appreciation has continually grown for her substantive leadership and sense of humor alike."
  • "I know there are people that run against each other for president and literally hate each other," Klobuchar, who's in her fourth term in the Senate but will leave in January to become Minnesota's governor, told Axios. "That was far from the case for us."

Flashback: A casual observer might see that as a bit of revisionist history.

  • The Buttigieg-Klobuchar spats during the 2020 Democratic primary were some of the most vicious of that campaign. Aides from both sides can still quote the barbs, word for word.
  • "I wish everyone was as perfect as you, Pete," Klobuchar sniped at one debate in Las Vegas before saying "You've memorized a bunch of talking points and a bunch of things."
  • She added after the debate that Buttigieg was "haughty" and that "given the guy [Trump] we have in the White House, maybe you need someone who's a little more humble."

Buttigieg repeatedly mocked Klobuchar for not remembering the name of the president of Mexico in an interview.

  • He said Klobuchar was "not able to speak to literally the first thing about the politics of the country to our south."
  • She shot back: "Are you trying to say that I'm dumb?"

Asked today about those mutual attacks, Klobuchar says simply: "We both wanted to win."

  • Many Democrats laughed that their feud appeared to continue into 2021, when the two wrote books with opposite titles — "Trust" by Buttigieg, and "Anti-Trust" by Klobuchar.
  • When Buttigieg announced recently that he has a book coming out in January titled "Next," he texted Klobuchar: "Please tell me you're not putting out a book called 'Last.'"

Zoom in: Klobuchar said their relationship has become increasingly warm through the years.

  • "We kept consistently in touch, and not just over work. We had lunch when he first got into Washington. I remember I saw their apartment at the time," she said. "I also worked with him extensively on transportation issues."
  • She added that she came to appreciate "how smart and even-keeled he is" at a time when "'hair on fire' is kind of cool to be."
  • Buttigieg, who campaigned with Klobuchar during the 2026 midterms, said he's "looking forward to seeing all that she accomplishes as governor, and also to my next opportunity to join her at the Minnesota State Fair."

What they're saying: A former Klobuchar aide told Axios that it's a "very Midwestern friendship story."

  • "You meet someone new with a healthy dose of competition, skepticism, and a little frostiness. And along the way, you find out you genuinely like each other. That's Amy and Pete."

What's next: Klobuchar, who has said she's not running for president, didn't want to weigh in on 2028 because she knows many people who are likely to run.

  • As for what she thinks of Buttigieg's potential candidacy: "He has always been impressive."
