Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year.

  • Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead.

Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey).

Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement.

  • Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then.
  • In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels.

The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.

item.title: What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous is the weapon
item.description:
President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats.

The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption.

Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it."

  • "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.
  • Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not."
  • Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack.

Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C.

  • CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack."
  • "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman.
  • Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless."

Read more about dirty bombs below.

What is a dirty bomb?

How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

  • This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says.

How dangerous is a dirty bomb?

The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

  • The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled.
  • "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says.
  • The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC.

Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast.

What would happen if one exploded in Washington?

Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats.

  • The Department of Homeland Security's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors.

DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks.

  • The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials.

Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site.

  • The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off.
  • Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says.
  • Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says.

Has a dirty bomb ever been used?

No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports, though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts.

  • The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia.
  • In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice. The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized.

The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

item.title: Scammers are sending fake emails to people worried about Nvidia's stock
item.description:
Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware.

Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat.

Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy.

  • Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices.
  • KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker.
  • KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added.

The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns.

  • Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said.
  • That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people.
  • AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said.

By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data.

  • In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours.
  • Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news or planned events impersonated a globally recognized brand, according to KnowBe4.

The bottom line: Palma recommends taking a closer look at any unexpected email that appears to reference breaking news, even if the headline seems familiar.

item.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
item.description:
Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday.

Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology.

  • Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees.

Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12, requesting they appear.

  • The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations.
  • Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed.

What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release.

  • "We look forward to meeting with the Chairmen on December 2," Nvidia said in a statement.
  • When reached for comment Tuesday, a representative for Huang pointed to a statement the former CEO made Tuesday about returning as CEO.

What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International.

  • Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips.
  • Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies.

The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have raised concerns from lawmakers about whether the government did enough to crack down on Nvidia's chips finding their way to China.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Jensen Huang acknowledged in a statement that he'd be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO.

Why it matters: A push to reinstate Huang began almost as soon as he exited the company, but Nvidia's board said it isn't currently considering reinstating the former CEO.

What they're saying: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang's statement said.

  • "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
  • The Wall Street Journal first reported Huang's statement.

Yes, but: Nvidia's board made clear Tuesday during its earnings call that Huang is not under consideration to return as CEO, AP reports.

State of play: Multiple analyses and reports have mentioned a slew of replacement candidates for Huang's successor at Nvidia.

  • President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the role. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look for outside candidates.
  • Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as the company's interim CEO.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang resigned as CEO after he allegedly had affairs with two Nvidia employees and former Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

  • Jensen Huang immediately faced Congressional backlash over whether Nvidia's AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether his company did enough to protect American tech.
  • He has agreed to testify before Congress next month, lawmakers said Tuesday.

Since he stepped down, Nvidia's stock has tumbled, and tech CEOs have questioned whether Jensen Huang should have been ousted in the first place.

  • His backers have included Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
  • Elon Musk has also backed the campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang, which has collected more than 180,000 signatures
  • Many supporters say that a lack of proof of the allegations about his relationship with Alice Huang is reason enough to reinstate him.

The other side: Nvidia's investigation into Jensen Huang's conduct is ongoing.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional context throughout.

item.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
item.description:
Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology.

  • That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday.

Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates.

  • Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders.

What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed.

  • Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research.
  • (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.)

Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups:

  1. Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices.
  2. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder.

The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses.

  • Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said.
  • Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming large parts of the economy, which he says would limit job losses and productivity gains.

"You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said.

  • "You can also view this as very negative. Productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate," he added.

The big picture: Warsh is turning to influential outsiders to challenge how the central bank thinks about the economy.

  • Affirm CEO Max Levchin told Warsh that AI has made the company's engineers five times more productive, cutting the cost of developing new features by 80%.
  • Stripe CEO Patrick Collison said new businesses launching on its platform each week have doubled from a year ago, an unprecedented surge in its 15-year history.
  • Unlike established companies, startups are more willing to let AI independently develop products and fix bugs, potentially allowing them to grow faster with fewer employees.

What to watch: Executives said AI is already delivering productivity gains in traditional industries — including sectors Andreessen said are more resistant to technological change.

  • Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, a large nonprofit health system, said AI tools that transcribe patient appointments are saving some physicians two to four hours a day on paperwork. Wexler said that one doctor called it "life-changing."

What's next: Warsh has asked all five task forces to recommend ways to improve Fed policymaking by year-end, though he cautioned last month that some may miss the deadline.

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries shifts tactics ahead of House Democrats' internal speaker vote
item.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as speaker of the House, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Why it matters: The plan represents a shift in tactics — his allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation — that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become speaker on Jan. 3.

  • If he loses more than 40 votes, he may be in trouble. If not, he likely sails through even if some of his members ultimately oppose him on the House floor.
  • Jeffries and his allies are confident he has more than enough support to get the 218 votes needed to become speaker even as some of his freshman members express skepticism or even outright opposition to him.
  • "Jeffries will win," a senior House Democrat told Axios.

Jeffries' plans were first reported by Punchbowl News.

Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker.

  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker.
  • Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported.
  • Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees: "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people."

State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress.

  • In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions.
  • Most of the candidates for those senior roles are running unopposed and are still expected to be elected by voice vote because "people don't want long votes," said the senior House Democrat.
  • Any recorded votes would still be secret ballots, unlike the Jan. 3 speaker vote in which members must stand on the floor and announce their choice.

Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker.

  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker.
  • Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported.
  • Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees: "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people."

State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress.

  • In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions.
  • Most of the candidates for those senior roles are running unopposed and are still expected to be elected by voice vote because "people don't want long votes," said the senior House Democrat.
  • Any recorded votes would still be secret ballots, unlike the Jan. 3 speaker vote in which members must stand on the floor and announce their choice.

item.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday.

Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it.

The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum.

  • Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus.
  • Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia.
  • Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector.

What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time.

  • "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts.
  • "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities.
  • "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions."

By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.)

Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion.

  • Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion.
  • The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge.

The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

item.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
item.description:
Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios

The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again, according to the latest March of Dimes report card.

Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life.

By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row.

  • It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%).

Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%.

  • Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data.
  • But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines.

Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios.

  • High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth.

What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course."

  • That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy.

What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

item.title: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool
item.description:
So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown, are foreseeable ... and foreseen.

Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits.

A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix.

  • A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital.

The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems.

Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades:

  1. The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks. We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion."
  2. The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break.
  3. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July, cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit.
  4. The government's computers: Washington spends over $100 billion a year on information technology. Roughly 80% goes to keeping old systems alive. Eight of the 11 systems most in need of replacement run on dying languages like COBOL. The people who can read, write and fix them are retiring.
  5. The debt: We paid $1.052 trillion in interest last fiscal year. That's more than we spent on defense. The Congressional Budget Office sees the interest doubling to $2.1 trillion in 2036. Every dollar of interest is a dollar that can't fix another crisis on this list.
  6. The retirement cliff: Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in 2032. Current law then cuts benefits by 22%, automatically. Medicare's hospital fund follows in 2033. We have known those dates for decades, and they've been creeping up. Now they're just a few years away.
  7. The shriveled arsenal: Rebuilding the advanced weapons we've burned through in the Iran war will take years. Back in May, a paper from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that replacing some interceptors used heavily in the war, including Patriot and THAAD anti-missile systems, would take three years.
  8. The minerals: China controls 91% of the world's rare-earth refining capacity, giving the other superpower a chokehold on vital ingredients of AI. We're one trade war away from slowing AI and the entire economy.

The bottom line: When choosing and rating leaders in harrowing times, put a premium on competence. We'll need it.

  • Go deeper: The chain-reaction era.

item.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
item.description:
The push to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable.

Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power.

  • Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore?
  • Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing.
  • "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergey Brin, told Bloomberg. "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable."

Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy.

  • President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Musk has also backed the effort.
  • Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
  • Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return.

Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset.

  • That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question.

Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips.

  • The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases and also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to the Wall Street Journal.
  • In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives.

Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic.

Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers.

  • In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO.
  • After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package, shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award.
  • Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable.

The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy.

  • But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward.
  • Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence.

The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal.

  • OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal.
  • Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct.
  • "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said.

Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg.

The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.

item.title: Democrats' squishy definition of Medicare expansion
item.description:
Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program.

Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive.

The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress.

  • Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like.
  • How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support.

Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto.

  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage.
  • House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported.
  • And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50.

What they're saying: "Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum.

State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other changes beyond changing the eligibility age.

  • More than a dozen Senate Democrats have introduced legislation capping Medicare out-of-pocket spending at $5,000 a year.
  • House Democrats' health care working group called for both a $5,000 out-of-pocket cap and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits within the first 100 hours of taking the House majority.

Between the lines: More sweeping proposals for a single-payer system would result in a Medicare program without premiums or patient cost-sharing. It would instead fund care with taxpayer dollars.

  • Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket.
  • This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan.
  • That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes.

What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all.

  • Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes.
  • They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency.
  • Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

  • Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket.
  • This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan.
  • That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes.

What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all.

  • Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes.
  • They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency.
  • Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

item.title: Trump's biggest project is running out of time
item.description:
Look past the White House renovations, the proposed arch and the golf course: President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace.

Why it matters: "Build that wall" helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished.

State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029.

  • There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10.
  • The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data.
  • But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms.

Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention.

  • "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands."

Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there.

  • The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border.
  • "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would make more sense to have the wall in," Flores said.
  • The General Land Office already reprimanded CBP and one of the border wall contractors for unauthorized construction in a cease-and-desist letter this July.

Between the lines: Trump faces two main fronts of legal fights.

  • Injunctions: More than a half dozen lawsuits are challenging the border wall in West Texas alone, building on legal fights elsewhere on the border and in Washington.
  • Eminent domain: If local private landowner resistance continues, the federal government will also have to file individual eminent domain cases for each plot of land across the border. It has already filed some of these cases, including one against a church in New Mexico.

Zoom out: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference this summer that he was planning for a physical wall from "the Pacific to the Gulf of America this time next year."

  • CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott gave an extended deadline to the end of 2027.
  • Based on data shared by CBP, there would need to be a rapid increase in construction tempo to make this possible.

What they're saying: Flores plans to tell administration officials to ease their aggressive timeline.

  • "Let's be a little bit more careful because you know this is gonna stand there for a long time. Let's understand those ramifications a little bit more. But that is not to say that I'm not willing to explore all legal options at my disposal to make sure I am defending the best interests of Texas," he said.

The other side: After publication, CBP spokesperson Hilton Beckham said in a statement to Axios that the agency expects construction pace to increase and primary wall construction to be finished by January 2028.

  • Art Del Cueto, a former Border Patrol agent and adviser at the immigration restriction group FAIR, argues that the border wall needs to stick to the original plan.
  • "Now you've heard other individuals saying, 'Well, maybe we don't need it where you have natural barriers,' and that's understandable. But when you don't build in those areas, what it's going to do is it's going to create a funnel," Del Cueto said.

item.title: Florida stayed red in a blue wave. But look at what happened in Hispanic precincts.
item.description:
Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found.

  • Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly.

Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold.

  • "There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios.
  • "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat."

The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of.

  • Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades.
  • Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains.

State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race.

  • Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024.
  • The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35) and Mexican and Central American ones (D+3 to D+44).

The intrigue: Outside of Tampa, democratic socialist Ashley Herrmann flipped state House District 69.

Zoom in: The swing was particularly noticeable in the Cuban American core of Miami-Dade.

  • In precincts where 75% or more of the voter base is Cuban, voters favored Nixon slightly more than they did Jolly, data show.
  • Nixon lost Hialeah by 31 points. Demings lost it by 59 in 2022, and Mucarsel-Powell by 53 in 2024.
  • She lost Westchester by 34 points and Tamiami by 33, down from 55 and 54 in 2022.

Between the lines: Jolly outperformed Nixon statewide, but only because he had stronger support among white voters and in the most Jewish precincts of Miami-Dade, Palm Beach and Broward counties.

  • The left-wing Nixon held her own with Hispanic voters, though the party's Hispanic statewide nominees did better.
  • In Hispanic-majority precincts, Nixon ran slightly ahead of moderate governor nominee Jolly (losing them by 2.8 points to his 3.2) but behind attorney general nominee José Javier Rodríguez, CFO nominee Annette Taddeo and agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins.
  • By Axios' estimates, Nixon ran about 3 points ahead of Jolly among Black and Hispanic voters and about 4 points behind him among white voters.

The results could mean the anti-communist and anti-socialist attacks against Nixon resonated less this year — the result of Trump's immigration efforts, Smith said.

  • "The sentiments are still there, but it'll be interesting to see if [the results] were a wholesale move away from the Republican Party for those who turned out to vote or a backlash against the overzealous anti-immigration efforts by the Trump administration," he said.

Yes, but: The results still don't have "the full picture" of who actually voted on Election Day, Democratic strategist Steve Schale told Axios Monday.

  • They don't show if some Cubans found Nixon or Jolly's comments appealing versus other Cubans simply not showing up to vote, he said.
  • An Axios analysis found ballots cast in Miami-Dade precincts where most voters were born in Cuba fell 3% from 2022, while they rose 7% countywide.

The bottom line: For Schale, Democrats must focus on the "gap," or what it will take to lose a Hispanic precinct by 20 points instead of 30.

item.title: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
item.description:
President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious.

Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats.

  • "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios.
  • Substance aside, Western diplomats worry about the optics of Trump appearing alongside two emboldened strongmen. On Monday, Trump also floated a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?"

  • But other topics will get attention, too, Trump went on to say.
  • "We'll talk about Iran. We have Iran in very good shape, but we'll talk about Iran a little bit," he said.
  • The president also said "we'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine."
  • His comments came after U.S. officials stressed in a call with reporters on Friday that the summit would not deal with the war in Ukraine. Chinese officials said the same thing.

Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine.

Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat.

  • Some of them raised concerns about what Trump might say about the war in Ukraine, the diplomat said.
  • German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among the more vocal during the private session. He then went out and spoke about it publicly.
  • "Our message to the U.S. before Trump meets Putin is: No surprises, please," Merz said.
  • Ukrainian officials expressed similar worries.
  • Japanese officials also privately relayed concerns to U.S. counterparts about the message the summit might project about Washington's stance on Taiwan or Asia more broadly, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. A potential public meeting between Trump and Kim Jong Un would be even more concerning for Japan.

The intrigue: European diplomats said U.S. officials tried to downplay the summit and lower expectations about any substantive results.

  • But many of the U.S. allies are nervous that the meeting will project an image of the three leaders scheming to carve up the earth into spheres of influence. Some of them invoked "Yalta II" — referring to the 1945 summit between the U.S., Great Britain and the Soviet Union that helped shape post-war Europe.

State of play: On the same day Trump meets with Xi and Putin, his envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to be in Berlin with senior officials from Ukraine, Germany, France, the UK, Italy, Poland, the EU and NATO, according to two sources.

  • The purpose is to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi the following week.
  • On Monday, Kushner and Witkoff held a virtual meeting with the representatives of the different entities.
  • "We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years. It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe," Kushner wrote on X.

The other side: Witkoff and Kushner also spoke on Monday with Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the peace process.

  • The White House said Putin had agreed to allow European representatives to join the negotiations with Ukraine and to launch a parallel track of talks regarding a Europe-Russia security deal.
  • But Ushakov said no such agreement had been reached.

item.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
item.description:
President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said.

Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close.

  • On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine.

Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said.

  • The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said.
  • The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said.

Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks.

  • Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement.
  • Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire.

The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war.

  • Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that Europe would have a seat at the table, but Ushakov said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

item.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
item.description:
One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership.

Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership.

  • The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios.

Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes, a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic.

  • Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision.
  • Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings.
  • Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals.

The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress.

  • One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference.
  • Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes.
  • "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal.

Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October.

  • A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals.

The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in.

  • But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation.
  • "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said.

What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal.

  • "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year."
  • "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it.

Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress.

But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda.

  • "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios.
  • "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added.
  • "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios.

What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership.

Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership.

  • The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios.

Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes, a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic.

  • Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision.
  • Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings.
  • Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals.

The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress.

  • One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference.
  • Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes.
  • "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal.

Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October.

  • A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals.

The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in.

  • But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation.
  • "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said.

  • "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios.

What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

item.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
item.description:
United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes.

Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop.

What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer.

  • "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com. Thanks for bearing with us!"
  • The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem.

United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights."

  • "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said.
  • About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website.
  • United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
item.description:
Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns.

Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students.

  • Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce.

Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education.

  • Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students.
  • International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates.
  • However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%.

Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios.

  • She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities.
  • "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues."
  • Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships.

By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars.

  • Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators.
  • That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported.
  • It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth.

Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing.

Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

  • International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk.
  • Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report.

Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition.

  • Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students.
  • A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices.

Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit.

  • The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue.

The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent.

  • "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect."

Go deeper: What to know about the wave of student visa cancellations

item.title: How one router may have grounded thousands of U.S. flights
item.description:
A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide.

Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel.

Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said, with thousands more delayed.

  • "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday.

Read more below.

What caused the nationwide groundstop?

What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds."

  • Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal.
  • The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris, has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide.

After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA.

  • "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement.

How did a router disrupt flights nationwide?

How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft.

  • The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft.
  • A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications.

The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds.

  • The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights.

What to know about radio frequency outages

One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions.

  • Some reports described this as a "rolling frequency outage," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time.
  • This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers.

Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy.

What happens to pilots during the outages?

Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail.

  • These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual.
  • The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage.
  • Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities.

Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected.

What does this mean for flights?

Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions.

  • Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports.
  • Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft.

What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris.

  • The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.
